name: communities
description: Every community this instance knows about, its own included. The home community is the row with foreign = false; there is exactly one.

columns.name: remote
columns.description: false on exactly one row: this instance's own community. Everything else is known by reference.
columns.note: Legacy calls it `foreign`, which is a reserved word in PostgreSQL and not even parseable unquoted in SQLite, so every hand-written query in both implementations would have to remember the quotes. `remote` is a keyword in neither and says the same thing. The word in conversation stays 'foreign community' — that is a vocabulary the column no longer matches, which is the whole cost of the change.

columns.name: url
columns.description: Base URL of the community. Unique.

columns.name: public_key
columns.description: ed25519 public key. Legacy stored it hex-encoded in a binary(64) column until migration 0068 turned it into the 32 raw bytes it always was.

columns.name: private_key
columns.description: Only the home community carries one. A foreign row with a private key is a bug.

columns.name: community_uuid
columns.description: The community's public identity: what federation names it by, and the only place a community uuid is stored.
columns.note: A real uuid, always — a reader may assume it. Legacy parks a uint32 one-time pass code in this char(36) column during community authentication, which is why an earlier version of this file could not commit to the type; that was replaced by the community handshake, and the code now lives in community_handshake_states.one_time_code where it belongs. Because the column is NOT NULL, communities_uuid_key is a constraint that actually holds: two NULLs are distinct in a unique index, so a nullable version of this column would have enforced nothing.
columns.open: Several tables still join a community by uuid — transactions.user_community_uuid, user_aliases.community_uuid, crea_records.community_uuid, pending_transactions. users was moved to a row id (users.community_id) and the rest are intended to follow, but each has to be checked before it is changed.

columns.name: authenticated_at
columns.description: When the handshake with this community last succeeded.

columns.name: creation_date
columns.description: When the community itself was founded — not when this row was written. created_at is that.

columns.name: location
columns.open: Same unresolved column as users.location — MariaDB geometry with a custom transformer, and neither PostgreSQL without PostGIS nor SQLite has an answer. Decide once, for both tables.

columns.name: hiero_topic_id
columns.description: The Hiero consensus topic this community publishes to.
columns.note: Legacy's entity declares varchar(255) while migration 0092 created varchar(512); the database is the longer one. Written here at 512 — a shorter column would truncate on read-modify-write.

notes: Rows are joined by community_uuid and by public_key, almost never by id. An implementation that treats id as the community identity will not match legacy data.
Timestamps are UTC milliseconds; see types/Timestamp.json. This table uses datetime(3) throughout, so sub-second ordering is real here — unlike contributions and transaction_links.
A private key lives in this table. It must never be selected by a query that also feeds a response, and never logged. See logging.json.

public_key is unique. Legacy intended it — migration 0065 created UNIQUE KEY public_key_key — and migration 0068 lost the constraint while widening the column, so the live legacy schema does not enforce it. gradido2 repairs that rather than inheriting it: public_key is what the federation handshake identifies a community by, and two rows holding one key is not a duplicate, it is an authentication ambiguity. A community that wants a new key rotates the column; it does not get a second row.
